symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Run a congestion heatmap with pin-density overlay for the worst DRC areas
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest visual clue to separate macro-pin blockage from logic-cell congestion

first_checks.check: Check the routed layer distribution (which metal layers are saturated) in the DRC cluster
first_checks.why_first: Rules out whether the issue is via density vs. horizontal/vertical track shortage

first_checks.check: Verify whether the DRCs correlate with clock-net shielding or wide-metal power stripes that force detours
first_checks.why_first: These are structural, not placement-driven, and have a distinct fix

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add a partial placement blockage over the DRC area, run a quick global route, and compare overflow; if overflow drops >50%, the root is cell-macro proximity; if unchanged, it's fixed obstacle routing
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Overflow unchanged points to fixed obstacles or routing geometry

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Manually route the top 5 most congested nets through the area with modified spacing rules; if they route without DRC, it's a default rule issue; if they fail, it's global track starvation
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Rule modification passes means DRC is due to conservative design-rule defaults
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Fails even with relaxed spacing indicates absolute track shortage

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare DRC cluster to the global-route congestion map; if global route predicted low congestion but detail route fails, suspect pin-access or via-stack restrictions
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Low predicted + high DRC = pin-access/via issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: High predicted = valid global-route prediction, need floorplan change

common_root_causes.cause: Macro pin blockage / pin density at hard-macro boundaries
Clock net shielding and power grid metal cutting available routing tracks
Non-default routing rules (NDR) for critical nets creating oversized keep-out zones
Via-stack restrictions due to multi-patterning coloring conflicts
Placement density metric ignoring pin-access complexity (local cell-legalization hotspots)

classic_trap: Assuming it's a placement-density problem and respreading cells, when the real cause is pin-access blockage from adjacent macros or fixed power stripes.
node_era_note: At 7nm and below, via-pillar and cut-layer coloring constraints dominate, whereas at 28nm the fix is usually track utilization and cell-layer flipping.

first_checks.check: Check the slack histogram for a single common clock-gating cell or latch at the root of many failing paths
first_checks.why_first: Immediately discriminates local skew vs. global clock latency distribution

first_checks.check: Compare the pre-CTS setup slack with post-CTS slack for the same endpoint group
first_checks.why_first: Reveals whether CTS worsened insertion delay or changed logic-update criticality

first_checks.check: Check whether the violating paths share a common data-mux or bus structure that crossed a partition boundary
first_checks.why_first: Points to cross-hierarchy RC delay, not clock skew

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Extract all failing paths and group by common clock root; if 80% share one gater, the cause is late clock arrival at that gater; if they spread across unrelated gaters, it is data-path or library variation
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Common gater confirms skew or insertion-delay imbalance at that gater
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Spread across gaters points to global OCV or PVT corner mismatch

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Hold the clock tree fixed, run a data-only incremental optimization with 10% more drive strength on the common data-buffer chain; if slack improves >50%, root is weak data buffers (slew degradation); if little change, root is clock latency

Compare the failing path’s clock insertion delay to the ideal target; if all failing endpoints are late by the same 20ps offset, it is systematic – due to CTS target mismatch; if delays are random, it is OCV

common_root_causes.cause: Clock gater insertion delay imbalance – gaters placed too far from clock root
Overly optimistic pre-CTS wireload model that under-estimated data-path RC
Sudden OCV derate jump at the post-CTS corner that was not applied during placement
Cross-hierarchy data bus with high coupling capacitance that became real after detailed routing

classic_trap: Blaming the CTS clock tree for setup when the data path actually shifted due to placement changes during clock-tree synthesis – run a data-path delay comparison first.
node_era_note: At 7nm, setup is heavily affected by via-resistance and middle-of-line RC, requiring early clock vs data co-optimization; at 28nm, the fix is usually a simpler buffer-size push.

first_checks.check: Check if all hold violations are on short paths between flip-flops that share the same clock leaf (same buffer chain)
first_checks.why_first: This is the cheapest way to rule out skew vs. data-path min-delay

first_checks.check: Check if the violations correlate with clock early-arrival at the capturing flop vs. launch flop (skew direction)
first_checks.why_first: Immediately tells if it's a CTS balancing error vs. data-buffer insertion

first_checks.check: Check if the violating paths have clock gater insertion delays that are negative relative to target
first_checks.why_first: Gater early-arrival is a known systematic hold source

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add 10ps of intentional delay on the common data path of all failing endpoints (via buffer insert) in an ECO; if all violations clear, the root is insufficient data-path delay; if they persist, root is clock skew.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Data delay fixes all = data path too short
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Data delay does not fix = skew
discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run a skew report on the launch-capture pair for each failing path; if the skew (launch - capture) is negative by more than 5ps for all, root is clock tree imbalance; if skew is positive, root is data min-delay.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Negative skew consistent = clock tree imbalance

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Isolate paths that cross clock domains versus same-domain; if cross-domain are dominant, it's a clock-domain crossing synchronizer issue, not a general hold problem.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Cross-domain dominate = synchronizer or clock-gating scheme
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Same-domain dominate = local clock or data issue

common_root_causes.cause: Clock skew: launch clock too early relative to capture due to unbalanced tree at that leaf
Data path actually has too few buffers because the synthesis tool removed them for area
Hold margin not accounting for clock-gater insertion delay that is negative (gater placed close to root)
Clock reconvergence with different global tree paths creating a large local skew

classic_trap: Trying to fix hold by adding data-path delay globally, when the real cause is a skew reversal that can be fixed by rebalancing one clock buffer – check skew direction per endpoint first.
node_era_note: At 7nm, hold is dominated by via-metal RC mismatch in the clock tree (systematic variation) and requires on-chip variation (OCV) derates specific to each metal layer; at 28nm, it's usually fixed with simple buffer insertion in data path.

first_checks.check: Overlay the timing-critical path's instance location on the static IR-drop map – see if drop >5% at those instances
first_checks.why_first: Instantly confirms IR as primary cause vs. unrelated OCV

first_checks.check: Check if the failing paths occur in a small dense region (e.g., near a core corner or next to a hard macro) that is far from power pads
first_checks.why_first: Rule out global vs. local drop

first_checks.check: Check the toggle rate of the logic in that region – if low, it's static IR; if high, it's dynamic IR (di/dt)
first_checks.why_first: Different fix: static needs extra stripes, dynamic needs decap

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run a vector-less static IR analysis with a 2x increased current density in that region; if timing fails degrade proportionally, it's static IR; if not, run a vector-based dynamic analysis – if dynamic shows high peak, it's switching activity
Insert a small decap (in simulation) at the failing instance and rerun timing; if slack recovers >80%, root is dynamic IR; if not, root is insufficient power-grid density
Increase supply voltage by 5% in simulation for the failing path; if slack fully recovers, then IR is the dominant factor; if only partial, then OCV or RC also contribute.

common_root_causes.cause: Insufficient power-grid density in that region (missing straps or vias)
High local switching activity (toogle rate) causing dynamic voltage droop
Resistance of the power network due to EM-limited narrow metal and long resistance from the pad
Inadequate decoupling capacitance (both on-chip and off-chip) for the clock-gating activity

classic_trap: Assuming it's a static IR drop and adding power stripes, when the actual cause is a dynamic di/dt event from a huge clock-gater toggling – adding decap is far cheaper.
node_era_note: At 7nm, dynamic IR is much more severe due to finFET drive strength and higher current density, requiring time-domain analysis; at 28nm, static IR map is usually sufficient.

symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Check the insertion delay histogram – see if the diverging sinks are all driven by a single clock-gater or a specific level of the tree
first_checks.why_first: Narrows root to a specific buffer branch or level

first_checks.check: Check the physical location of the diverging sinks relative to the clock root – if they are far from the center, it may be RC variation
first_checks.why_first: Separates systematic distance from random variation

first_checks.check: Check if the skew discrepancy is in the same direction (all late or all early) or mixed; if all late, it's a target-setting issue; if mixed, it's H-tree mismatch
first_checks.why_first: Target error vs. structural asymmetry

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run CTS with a different target insertion delay (e.g., +50ps) for that subtree; if divergence reduces, it's a target-spec issue; if not, it's RC variation.
Check the clock buffer sizing in the diverging branch; if all buffers are the same size as the other branches, the issue is wire RC; if they are undersized, it's buffer selection mismatch.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Same sizes = wire RC; different = buffer sizing error
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If same but still diverts, confirm RC

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Swap the clock root input to a different clock source (if available); if divergence follows the source, it's a source-jitter or PLL issue; if stays with the sinks, it's the tree itself.

common_root_causes.cause: Asymmetric RC due to non-uniform metal density or power-grid obstruction in one quadrant
Improper target insertion delay specification (overly aggressive) for that branch's physical length
Clock-gater insertion delay mismatch caused by different gater fanouts
Variation in via resistance (systematic) due to multi-patterning in that metal layer

classic_trap: Assuming it is a random OCV issue and increasing derates, when the divergence is systematic and can be fixed by rebalancing one branch – check the histogram mode first.
node_era_note: At 7nm, clock skew is dominated by via metal resistivity variation (especially via-0) and requires layout-based via optimization; at 28nm, wire length is the main factor.

symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Check the LVS report for the exact net names with shorts – see if they are supply nets (VDD/VSS) or signal nets
first_checks.why_first: Immediately tells if it's a power-rail short (usually a via punch) vs. signal bridge

first_checks.check: Check if the missing net is a high-fanout net (clock or reset) that may have been merged during power-grid synthesis
first_checks.why_first: Clock nets often get shorted to shield wires

first_checks.check: Check if the open net connects to a macro pin that has an internal layer mis-match (e.g., macro LEF vs. GDS layer mapping)
first_checks.why_first: This is a common interface error

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Extract the physical location of the shorted nets and overlay them with the power-grid via patterns – if the short is exactly under a power via, it's a via-to-signal spacing violation; if not, it's a routing bridge

Open the suspect net and run a connectivity trace to all pin connections; if the net connects to pins that are not in the netlist, it's a design-level missing port; if it connects to correct pins but with a gap, it's a broken track
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Gap = open via or broken wire

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run a short isolation test by comparing the GDS layers – if the short appears between metal1 and metal2, check via1 enclosure; if missing, it's a via misalignment

common_root_causes.cause: Power and signal nets crossing with insufficient spacing (spacing DRC missed due to routing grid shift)
Via-to-signal short from a power via dropped on a signal track during power-grid synthesis
Open connection due to a missing via at a hard-macro boundary (different layers)
Netlist mismatch between schematic and layout due to renamed net (e.g., net vs. net1) but LVS uses name-based matching

classic_trap: Blaming the router for a short when the LVS report shows a missing net – often the missing net is the same as the short net, and the real cause is a single misrouted wire that bridges two supplies – check the netlist first.
node_era_note: At 7nm, shorts and opens are often due to multi-patterning coloring errors (cuts layer) rather than typical metal bridging; at 28nm, it's almost always a DRC rule violation.

symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Check if the mismatched device is a FET that has a different L (length) or W (width) – is it a standard-cell internal device or a custom macro?
first_checks.why_first: Standard-cell mismatch usually due to library characterization vs. layout GDS; custom macro due to schematic mistake

first_checks.check: Check if the extra device is a small parasitic FET (e.g., dummy) or a full logic transistor – if dummy, it's a dummy-insertion mismatch; if logic, it's a netlist bug
first_checks.why_first: Dummies are common in I/O or analog blocks

first_checks.check: Check if the device orientation (finger vs. multi-finger) causes a size mismatch but total area matches – LVS sometimes reports as wrong size
first_checks.why_first: Different layout style but same electrical can be harmless

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare the schematic netlist (CDL) and the layout-extracted netlist (SPICE) for that device's terminals – if terminals are swapped (source/drain), it's a pin-order mismatch; if W/L differ, it's a layer/parameter extraction issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Terminal swap = pin mapping error; W/L diff = extraction rule error
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If both match but still wrong, it's a device-type mismatch (e.g., native vs. low-Vt)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Remove all filler cells and dummy devices from the layout in simulation and rerun LVS; if the mismatch disappears, it's dummy-insertion; if persists, it's a logic device
Check if the extra device is connected only to VDD and VSS with no gate connection – that is a decap capacitor, often inserted by the power-grid tool; if so, it can be waived

common_root_causes.cause: Library standard-cell GDS vs. schematic device size mismatch due to different versions (e.g., L=0.13um vs 0.15um)
Dummy transistor insertion in I/O or analog blocks not reflected in netlist
Multi-fingered transistor layout where LVS tool incorrectly counts fingers as separate devices
Parasitic diode or resistor extracted as a device but not in schematic

classic_trap: Assuming a device size mismatch is a layout bug, when the real cause is that the schematic has a different L due to the designer using a non-default threshold-voltage cell – always check library variant first.
node_era_note: At 7nm, device size mismatches often involve fin count (number of fins) rather than W/L, and the extraction rule must correctly map fins to width; at 28nm, W/L is straightforward.

first_checks.check: Check the antenna report for the exact metal layer and net – are violations on long wires connected to gate oxides without a diode?
first_checks.why_first: Immediately identifies if it's a known long-wire net (clock, reset) vs. a short local interconnect

first_checks.check: Check if the violating net has a diode already placed but far away – if so, it's a jump-over diode, not a missing diode
first_checks.why_first: Antenna rule is about accumulated area during processing, not final net length

first_checks.check: Check if the violation is on a layer that is higher than the gate contact (e.g., metal4) – if so, the chance of real antenna damage is low (upper layers are processed after gate is protected)
first_checks.why_first: Many signoff tools report all layers, but only lower layers are critical

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check the antenna ratio (metal area / gate area) for each violating net; if the ratio exceeds the foundry limit only on metal1 or metal2, it's a real lower-layer antenna; if the ratio is high only on metal5, it's a false positive (since upper layers are processed after gate protection)
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: High-layer high ratio = false positive, can waive

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add a reverse-biased diode at the receiver gate (in simulation) and rerun antenna check; if violation clears, the fix is local; if not, the issue is with the jumper or bridge
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Diode doesn't clear = another structural issue (e.g., via chain)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare the antenna violation to the detailed routing structure; if the net has a large via stack (multiple vias in series), the via area might be double-counted – check if the tool counts via layers cumulatively
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Double-counting via area = tool setup issue

common_root_causes.cause: Long clock or reset nets routed on metal1 or metal2 without a diode at each gate input
Antenna diode placed too far (jumper) so that the intermediate wire segment still violates during processing
Signal nets that changed to higher metal layers during optimization, leaving lower-layer stubs connected to gates
Tool misconfiguration reporting antenna for all layers instead of only layers up to the gate-protection layer

classic_trap: Adding diodes to every violation, when many are false positives due to upper-layer metal or non-gate-terminated nets – check the critical layer filter first.
node_era_note: At 7nm, the antenna effect is more severe due to thinner gate oxide, but the foundry also provides more diode types and the rule is usually limited to metal1-3; at 28nm, it's a classic fix with diode insertion.

symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Check if the DRC hotspots are all around macro corners or near power-grid stripes
first_checks.why_first: These are known fixed obstacles that global routing underestimates

first_checks.check: Check if the violations are for minimum spacing or enclosure (e.g., via enclosure) – spacing vs. enclosure has different fixes
first_checks.why_first: Spacing can be fixed by wire spreading; enclosure requires via size change

first_checks.check: Check if the DRCs correlate with a specific metal layer that has a high via density from clock shielding
first_checks.why_first: Clock shielding adds extra parallel wires that cause spacing issues

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run a detailed-route with an increased wire-spacing rule (e.g., 2x spacing) only in the hotspot window; if the DRCs persist, it's a via or enclosure issue; if they disappear, it's a spacing issue
Remove the clock shielding from that region in a test run; if DRCs drop significantly, root is shielding-induced track starvation; if unchanged, it's logic net congestion

Check the global-route overflow map for that region; if global route overflow was zero but DRC exists, the root is pin-access or routing track alignment at the cell boundary – not a true capacity issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Positive overflow = capacity issue that global route missed

common_root_causes.cause: Pin-access blockage – the detailed router cannot find legal routing tracks to reach a cell pin due to orthogonal layer restrictions
Clock shielding wires causing excessive local density and spacing DRCs
Via enclosure rule violations because the via array is too close to the cell boundary
Multi-patterning coloring conflicts that were not considered in global route

classic_trap: Assuming the global route was correct and treating the DRC as a routing bug, when it's actually a pin-access problem that requires cell flipping or layer assignment changes – global route ignores pin geometry.
node_era_note: At 7nm, detailed-route hotspots are dominated by multi-patterning cut-layer coloring and via-resistance rules, requiring color-aware routing; at 28nm, it's usually simple spacing vs. enclosure.

symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Check the total cell area relative to the core area – if utilization >85%, it's likely a density limit
first_checks.why_first: Quick sanity check for fundamental capacity

first_checks.check: Check the overflow histogram for a specific macro or partition that has extremely high pin density
first_checks.why_first: Narrows to a specific block that is overpopulated

first_checks.check: Check if the overflow is on a single side of the chip (e.g., near the right edge) – could be a placement blockage from power grid or I/O
first_checks.why_first: Spatial bias indicates a fixed obstacle

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run a placement with a 20% larger core area (virtual) by adding padding; if overflow drops to zero, the root is absolute density; if still high, it's a structural blockage (macros)
Remove all hard macros from the design and run placement; if overflow disappears, the root is macro placement causing a ‘squeeze’ effect; if remains, it's cell-area overflow
Check if the unroutable area is exactly over an array of filler cells or tap cells – those can be placed elsewhere; if removing them frees enough tracks, the root is excessive filler density

common_root_causes.cause: Overall core utilization exceeding the practical routable limit (typically ~70-75% for high performance, 85% for low performance)
Hard macro placement creating narrow corridors that break global routing
High pin density on macros (e.g., memory) that consume all routing tracks near the macro boundary
Placement guidelines that forced cells to specific layers, causing local track overflow

classic_trap: Blowing up the core area or reducing cell count, when the real problem is a single macro placed badly, creating a choke point – check macro-to-macro spacing first.
node_era_note: At 7nm, unroutable placement is often due to finFET width quantization and pin accessibility constraints that are stricter than density; at 28nm, it's usually just density and macro spacing.
